summary: Cape St. George Light, an 1852 brick tower on Little St. George Island, Florida, fell into the Gulf in 2005; a rebuilt light now stands on St. George Island.

access.note: The rebuilt light on St. George Island is open to visitors at posted hours. The historic site on Little St. George Island was reachable only by boat (Florida Lighthouse Association).

events.note: First tower into service near the entrance to Apalachicola Bay (NRHP); the Florida Lighthouse Association places it near West Pass
NRHP: the first tower was rebuilt in 1847. The Florida Lighthouse Association and the county history date a second tower to 1848 (see resolved_conflicts)
Second tower completed farther east, per the Florida Lighthouse Association and the county history
NRHP: tower damaged by destructive winds in 1851. County history: the second tower fell in a hurricane in 1851. The 1 January 1852 notice says the lights were entirely swept away in a gale
Present brick tower erected (NRHP; archive gives 1852 as the tower year)
Civil War (1861-1865): the nomination says rebels damaged the tower; it was repaired. No date given
First-order oil house completed in December 1894 under contract (Light-House Board report, year ended 30 June 1895)
Materials furnished for the keeper to build a storm house (Light-House Board report, year ended 30 June 1900)
32-foot section of wharf built at the inner end of the old wharf (Light-House Board report, year ended 30 June 1901)
Keeper Clairmon Brooks rendered assistance when an auxiliary schooner grounded near the station, 31 July
Keeper Clairmon Brooks gave help to a British schooner short of provisions, 28 January (Bulletin 1923 volume)
Assistant keeper W. A. Roberts, jr., helped with a grounding near the lighthouse dock, late December 1927
Dwelling and other buildings on the reservation destroyed by fire
Light discontinued; taken out of service by the Coast Guard
Hurricane Opal caused the tower to tilt (AP)
Tower righted with a new foundation, summer 2000 (Florida Lighthouse Association). The AP gives 2002 for the tilt fix (see resolved_conflicts)
Tower toppled into the Gulf; found on Friday, 21 October 2005
Reconstruction on St. George Island opened to the public 1 December 2008 (county history); the Florida Lighthouse Association says it opened in 2008
Restored as a private aid to navigation by the Coast Guard on 1 November 2009; the rebuilt light was lit in 2009 (Florida Lighthouse Association)

corrections.why: The brick tower the record describes as standing is the 1852 tower. The archive gives 1852 as the year its tower was established, and the nomination dates the present tower to 1852. The 1833 tower was the first light on the cape.

corrections.proposed: collapsed 2005; rebuilt 2008 on St. George Island
corrections.why: The 1852 tower fell into the Gulf in October 2005. The light now shining is a rebuilt tower at a different site.

The Coast Guard restored the rebuilt light as a private aid to navigation on 1 November 2009, per the Florida Lighthouse Association, which describes it as seasonal. Human check: the map point is the historic site, and the rebuilt light is elsewhere.
The archive gives the light as 72 ft above mean high water for the 1852 tower, and the association gives a 72 ft focal plane for the rebuilt light. Neither source gives 23.0 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 2009 first light is the rebuilt light on St. George Island. The historic station was first lit in 1833 (NRHP; archive).
The 1994 discontinuance is the same in the archive (1994), the Florida Lighthouse Association (mid 1994) and the AP (1994). The 2009 restoration is a separate, later event.

notes_for_editor: Location: the record's point (29.587556, -85.047033) is the 1852 site on Little St. George Island; the archive places it at 29 deg 35.2 min N, 85 deg 2.8 min W, and its roster matched by name and position (0.10 km). The rebuilt light stands on St. George Island at about 29.663 N, 84.863 W (Florida Lighthouse Association), roughly 20 km from the record point. Editor to decide which point the map should show. CONFLICTS LEFT OPEN: rebuilding date 1847 (NRHP) against 1848 (FLA, county history); tower height 70 ft (NRHP), 72 ft to the light (archive), 74 ft (AP, 2005), 72 ft and 74 ft within the FLA page, 77 ft (Wikipedia, not cited). Tilt repair 2000 (FLA) against 2002 (AP). Collapse date 21 October 2005 (AP, FLA, county history); Wikipedia gives 22 October, not used. Reopening 1 December 2008 (county history) against fall 2008 (FLA). Dwelling 1878 (archive) against 1880 (NRHP). Builder 'Mr. E. Bowden' (NRHP) and 'Edward Bowden' (FLA) taken as the same person by the sources' context; the sources do not say so outright. Wikipedia-only facts NOT used in the story or JSON: $8,000 appropriation in 1847; the 1850 hurricane; lens removed to Apalachicola in the Civil War and reinstalled; lens replaced in 1899; 1878 tropical storm damage; mineral oil in 1882 and incandescent oil vapour in 1913; automated 1949; damage by Hurricane Georges in 1998; Samuel Parker keeper 1841-1842 (not in the archive roster). The USCG historian's page is blocked (403 through the Internet Archive). No primary source read gives the date of automation; the archive's roster ends with a principal keeper in 1946 and a first assistant in 1949, which the story reports as the archive's own span, not as an automation date. Range: NRHP gives '14 miles' with no unit; FLA gives '13 nautical miles' for the rebuilt light. Neither is recorded as range_nm. Characteristic 'Fl W 6s' in facts is the record's value; FLA dates the flash to 1977-1994. Clairmon Brooks: the 1926 Bulletin names a 'Clairmon Brooks' as keeper of the Apalachicola Range Light. The Bulletin does not link it to this station, so it is not put in other_stations and the story says so. Walter Roberts: the 1928 Bulletin text calls W. A. Roberts, jr., 'assistant keeper' at this station; the 1924-1929 Bulletin index calls 'Roberts, W.A.' keeper here. The archive lists 'Walter A. Roberts, Sr.' (1894-1913) and 'Walter Andrew Roberts' (1920-1938); the archive does not link them. OCR: the 1923 Bulletin's name for the British schooner is garbled ('Perceiver' per the scan's text), so the vessel name is not used. The 1928 Bulletin's date reads '2V' in the scan; the story says late December 1927. The 1901 report is cited by scan page 177; the printed page was not read. No woman keeper and no family member keeping the light in her own right is named in the sources read. The archive lists five men named Williams; the sources do not say whether they were related, and the story does not assume it. Not used: the 1921 Commissioner report line for repairs to the wharf, dwelling and walks ($2,021), whose year label is uncertain. Keepers: 50 lines copied from the archive (25 principal, 25 first assistant), each with its archive person slug from roster.py. No roster line is linked to another station. Visit facts (climbable, museum, opening hours) come from the Florida Lighthouse Association and the county history and may be out of date. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27 (independent check): the 1852 notice's replacement wait is given as 'within nine months or a year' (the notice says 'under 9 months or ene year'). The 1928 Bulletin day for W. A. Roberts, jr., is garbled in the scan ('December 2V and 30, 1927'), so the story says late December 1927 only. The 1926 Bulletin entry is read from OCR ('plunged into the water and r escued a boy from dr<;nvning'); the quote used is the clean part. The owner of the rebuilt light is not named by any source read, so the facts.agency field was removed. Page checks: the Light-House Board pages (scan 167, 142, 177) and the Bulletin PDF pages were checked against the corpus page index, and the Tribune notice text was read in the cache.
